title: Why singers wobble
teaches: The LFO: a slow oscillator that turns a knob for you, for vibrato, wah and tremolo

blocks.text: **The sound.** A synth note is dead straight: the same pitch from start to end, every time. That is what makes a cheap synth sound cheap. Below is that straight tone, and the same tone made to sing, the way a voice or a violin does. You will make the second from the first.

blocks.caption: A pulse wave held straight, and the same wave singing

blocks.text: Listen to an opera singer hold a long note. The pitch is not steady. It swings up and down five to seven times a second, sometimes by as much as a semitone either way. (A semitone is the step from one piano key to the next, black or white: about 6 percent in pitch.) Measured, the singer is hardly ever on the note. Yet the audience hears one clear pitch, the note itself, and hears it as richer and warmer than a dead-straight tone. Strings do the same: violinists rock a finger on the string to make a vibrato, and a cello section without one sounds pale and thin.

In the 1920s and 1930s the psychologist Carl Seashore and his students at the University of Iowa photographed thousands of sung notes as wavy traces on film, and found that good singers' vibratos were strikingly alike: about six cycles a second, about half a semitone each way (a full semitone from trough to peak).[^seashore] At that rate the ear doesn't track the wobble as a melody. It averages it into a pitch in the middle, and hears the movement as life.

A synth makes vibrato with a second oscillator too slow to hear as a tone, a **low-frequency oscillator** or **[[LFO]]**. It makes no sound itself. It turns a knob, up and down, over and over. Turning a setting this way is called **modulating** it.
**Depth** is how far the LFO turns its knob. Here it is wired to pitch. Start at zero and bring it up: first a gentle shimmer, then a singer's vibrato, then a seasick wobble no singer would allow.

blocks.caption: A pulse wave with the LFO wired to its pitch.

blocks.text: **Rate** is how fast the LFO goes round; one sweep is one full cycle, up and back. On this synth it is counted against the beat of the looping riff, from one sweep a bar (a bar is four beats) up to sixteen, so that a wobble stays in time with the music. It restarts each time the riff starts again, so when you match a sound, its wobble and yours always line up.

blocks.caption: The same vibrato. Change its rate.
blocks.task: Try the slowest rate and the fastest

blocks.text: Push an LFO fast enough, into the hundreds of cycles a second, and it stops being heard as a wobble at all. Something strange happens instead, which is lesson 6.

**Dest** is which knob the LFO turns. **Pitch** gives vibrato. **Cutoff** gives a wah, sweeping the brightness the way a wah-wah pedal or a mouth opening and closing does. **Width** sweeps the pulse width for a slow shimmer. **Level** turns the volume, which gives **tremolo**, a pulsing volume. Bigger synths drop this one-choice switch and let one LFO reach several of these at once, each by its own amount, through a *modulation matrix* (lesson 15).

Musicians have used the two words loosely for a century. Fender's amplifiers had a “vibrato” channel that wobbled the volume, which is tremolo, while their guitars had a “tremolo arm” that bent the pitch, which is vibrato.[^fender]

One famous machine does both at once. A **Leslie speaker**, made to go with the Hammond organ, has a horn that spins inside its cabinet. As the horn swings towards you, the sound waves arrive bunched together and the pitch rises; as it swings away they arrive stretched and the pitch falls. This is the **[[Doppler effect]]**, the same rise and fall you hear as an ambulance passes, and here it comes round a few times a second. At the same time the horn points at you, then away, so the volume pulses too.

blocks.caption: A Hammond B-3 organ with a Leslie 122 speaker beside it. The horn spins inside the top of the cabinet.

blocks.text: A horn tip moving at about 10 metres a second, against sound at 343, shifts the pitch by about 3 percent each way: roughly half a semitone. That is, by luck or design, the depth of a singer's vibrato.[^leslie]
Rate and depth together make most of the classic LFO sounds. A slow, deep sweep on the cutoff is a lazy wah. A fast, deep one is the wobbling bass of dubstep. Drag around the square to find them.

blocks.caption: Two knobs as one square: across is the rate, up is the depth, with the LFO on the cutoff.
blocks.task: Find a fast, deep wah: rate 1/8 (eight sweeps a bar) or quicker, depth 65 % or more

blocks.text: Now the singing tone from the start. Three questions, one for each knob. What is moving, the pitch, the brightness or the volume? How fast: a slow sway, or the quick shimmer Seashore measured, about six times a second? How far: a gentle half semitone, or a seasick swing? On this riff's tempo the quickest rate, sixteen sweeps a bar, is about seven a second.

blocks.caption: The LFO starts wired somewhere it shouldn't be. Set where it goes, how fast and how far, until your tone sings like the target.
blocks.task: Make the tone sing like the target

blocks.caption: Five questions on the LFO
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A good singer's vibrato swings the pitch about how often?
items.why: Seashore measured about six cycles a second, slow enough to be heard as movement but averaged into one pitch.

choices: Turns another knob up and down, over and over
items.why: A low-frequency oscillator is too slow to hear as a tone; it modulates another setting.

items.ask: An LFO on the volume gives which effect?
items.why: A pulsing level is tremolo; a wobbling pitch is vibrato; a sweeping cutoff is wah.

items.ask: Why does a Leslie speaker's spinning horn change the pitch?
choices: The Doppler effect, as the horn moves towards and away from you
The motor slows the organ down
items.why: A moving source bunches its waves ahead of it and stretches them behind, raising and lowering the pitch.

items.ask: An LFO is wired to the filter cutoff, deep and fairly fast. What do you hear?
choices: A wah that sweeps the brightness
items.why: Moving the cutoff opens and closes the brightness, like a wah pedal.

summary: **Singers wobble on purpose**: about six cycles a second, half a semitone each way, heard as one rich pitch.
**An LFO is an oscillator too slow to hear** that turns another knob for you.
**Depth is how far; rate is how fast.**
**Pitch gives vibrato, cutoff gives wah, level gives tremolo.**
**A Leslie speaker's spinning horn makes vibrato by the Doppler effect**, and tremolo as it turns towards you and away.

seashore.title: Seashore's films
seashore.text: Seashore's team built a “phonophotograph” that recorded the pitch of a voice as a trace on moving film, with the frequency marked on it, and measured every wiggle by hand. Their 1932 study of vibrato covered the great singers on record as well as students in the lab. Seashore also wrote some of the first tests of musical talent.

fender.title: Vibrato and tremolo, swapped
fender.text: The mix-up goes back to the 1940s and 1950s: Leo Fender called the volume effect in his amps vibrato and the pitch-bending bridge on his 1954 Stratocaster a synchronised tremolo. The names stuck, the wrong way round, and guitarists still say “whammy bar” to avoid the argument.

leslie.title: The Doppler shift, worked out
leslie.text: A source moving towards you at speed v raises the pitch by a factor of about 1 + v/c, where c is the speed of sound. With v = 10 m/s and c = 343 m/s that is 1.029, a rise of about 3 percent, and a semitone is 6 percent. A Leslie's horn turns at roughly 6 to 7 revolutions a second on its fast setting, which is also the rate of a singer's vibrato.
